attempts.raw_response: The confusion arises because the original Roman lituus was a straight or slightly curved ceremonial trumpet, while the Renaissance translators associated the term with the double-reed shawm family—instruments with a characteristic bulging middle and conical bore that produced a piercing, reedy sound. The German Krumhorn ("crooked horn") and Schalmey (from French chalemie) both refer to this instrument type, while the Italian trombetta bastarda and Spanish trompeta bastarda suggest a "bastard" or hybrid variant. This semantic drift reflects how Renaissance humanists, lacking physical examples of ancient instruments, often approximated classical terms using contemporary equivalents, sometimes quite inaccurately.

pair.human_continuation:
The early Baroque composer and author Michael Praetorius used the word as a Latin equivalent of the German "Schallmeye" (shawm) or for the "Krumbhoerner" (crumhorns)—in the latter case also offering the Italian translations storti, and cornamuti torti.

A more particular term, lituus alpinus, was used in 1555 by the Swiss naturalist Conrad Gessner when he published the earliest detailed description of the Alphorn: "nearly eleven feet long, made from two pieces of wood slightly curved and hollowed out, fitted together and skillfully bound with osiers".

A study made of Swedish dictionaries found that during the seventeenth century lituus was variously translated as sinka (= German Zink, cornett), krumhorn, krum trometa (curved trumpet), claret, or horn.
pair.prefix: A 1585 English translation of Hadrianus Junius's Nomenclator defines lituus as "a writhen or crooked trumpet winding in and out; a shaulme" (i.e., shawm), but a polyglot edition of the same book published in 1606 demonstrates how differently the term might have been understood in various languages at that time: German Schalmey, Krumme Trommeten, Krumhorn; Dutch Schalmeye; French Claron, ou cleron; Italian Trombetta bastarda; Spanish Trompeta curua, ò bastarda.
